newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian bourses continue recovery from last week.
newsitem.headline: Asian bourses continue recovery from last week.

text.p: HONG KONG - Asian stock markets on Tuesday extended their recovery from a correction last week as investors took heart in an overnight surge in New York stocks.

Investors, fuelling a second straight day of share-price gains, read the Dow's rise as a sign that U.S. markets had shrugged off last week's negative comments by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan, brokers said.
Tokyo's Nikkei 225 index climbed 218.41 points, or 1.06 percent, to close at 20,822.12, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index surged 198.23 points to close at 13,342.46, a gain of 1.51 percent.
Markets in Australia, Malaysia, Singapore, the Philippines and Taiwan also rose.
"We are moving in line with the Dow," said Peter Lai, associate director at OCBC Securities in Hong Kong.

The Dow Jones industrial average had jumped 82 points on Monday to 6,463.94, its biggest point gain in more than a month, after finance officials downplayed Greenspan's comments about "irrational exuberance" in financial markets.

Stock markets around the world interpreted the remarks as a hint that the Fed was poised to raise interest rates to keep the U.S. market from overheating, provoking a sell-off worldwide on Friday that was partially recouped on Monday.
"For the Tokyo market, the plunge of over 650 points last week may have been a blessing in disguise, providing it with energy to bounce back," said a broker.

Australian shares closed firmer, though brokers said the market's gain was slightly disappointing given the Dow's 82-point surge on Monday. The All Ordinaries index ended 22 points higher at 2,361.8, a gain of 0.94 percent.
Buyers filtered back into the Kuala Lumpur share market, lifting blue chips moderately and sending small-capitalisation counters sharply higher in subdued trading.
Building on session gains, the Composite Index closed up 11.22 points, or 0.93 percent, to 1,214.58, while the Second Board jumped 27.83 points, or 5.20 percent, to 562.77.
Singapore's Straits Times Industrials Index rose 12.37 points, or 0.56 percent. to close at 2,209.50 on the Dow's strength, brokers said.
"The market will continue to trade sideways. Wall Street will dictate the direction of the Singapore stock market for now," a dealer said.
Seoul stocks closed up 10.66 points, or 1.54 percent, at a provisional 702.83.
Taiwan share prices also finished slightly higher, but brokers said worries over possible inflation and a lack of market-boosting news had slowed buying interest.
The weighted index closed up 32.2 points, or 0.47 percent, at 6,841.03.
The Philippine equities market rebounded from a 1.57 percent drop on Monday, gaining back 38.22 points, or 1.24 percent, to close at 3,128.38 thanks to Wall Street, traders said.
Jakarta shares defied the regionwide optimism, slipping 7.90 points, or 1.24 percent, to close at 626.68, dragged down by falls in the share price of heavyweight Telkom.
The Thai stock market was closed for a holiday.

The dollar was firmer against the yen but off earlier highs and down against the mark in late Tokyo, while the pound remained sharply higher. At 1030 GMT, the dollar traded at 113.30/40 yen and 1.5554/59 marks.
After dull trading, Hong Kong gold bullion ended unchanged at US$367.90/368.40 an ounce against New York's US$367.90/368.30 close on Monday.
SIMEX Brent crude futures settled steady, but no trade was done as players held back, cautious and watchful of further Iraq news, brokers said.
The final resumption of Iraqi crude on Tuesday coupled with warmer than expected weather in the United States has weighed down prices, a broker said.
January Brent was last bid/offered at $23.84/$23.90 per barrel but settled untraded at $24.10, unchanged from its last International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) close.
